title: A Long Walk to Water (Selected Chapters & Dual Narratives)
author: Linda Sue Park
source: A Long Walk to Water: Based on a True Story (Clarion Books, 2010)
citation: Park, Linda Sue. A Long Walk to Water: Based on a True Story. Clarion Books / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2010.

sections.heading: Salva's Flight: Southern Sudan, 1985

epigraph.quote: Go into the bush, not back home! Run into the bush, do you hear me?
epigraph.attribution: —The Schoolteacher to Salva, A Long Walk to Water

paragraphs: Salva Dut was eleven years old, daydreaming in his village classroom in Loun-Ariik, when gunfire shattered the quiet afternoon. The Second Sudanese Civil War, fought between the northern Muslim government and southern rebels, had reached his quiet Dinka community. His teacher shouted above the cracks of rifles: 'Go into the bush! Don't run home—they will look for men and boys there!'

Leaving behind his books and his family, Salva fled into the wilderness with other villagers. For years, Salva marched across hundreds of miles of hostile terrain—surviving lion attacks, crossing the crocodile-infested Gilo River, and enduring blistering heat across the Akobo Desert. When his beloved Uncle Jewiir gave him a tamarind fruit and urged him forward one step at a time, Salva learned the mantra that kept him alive: take it one day, one step, at a time.

sections.heading: Nya's Journey: Southern Sudan, 2008

epigraph.quote: The sun was already baking the clay beneath her bare feet. Two hours there, two hours back. Every day.
epigraph.attribution: —Nya's Daily Walk, A Long Walk to Water

paragraphs: Twenty-three years later, in another part of Southern Sudan, an eleven-year-old Nuer girl named Nya begins her daily ritual. With a large plastic container balanced on her head, she walks two hours to a murky pond to collect muddy water for her family, returns home for a quick bowl of sorghum, and immediately turns back around to make the journey again.

Water dictates every hour of Nya's existence. During the dry season, her family moves to a lake camp, where she spends entire days digging holes in the cracked mud bed with her bare hands, waiting for dirty brown water to slowly seep into the hollow. Her younger sister Akeer falls severely ill from drinking contaminated water, forcing the family to walk days to a medical clinic.

sections.heading: The Meeting: Water for South Sudan

epigraph.attribution: —Salva to Nya, A Long Walk to Water

paragraphs: Years after surviving refugee camps in Ethiopia and Kenya, Salva was selected to be resettled in Rochester, New York, by an American family. While studying business and learning English, he learned that his father had miraculously survived the war but was dying from water-borne parasites in a remote Sudanese clinic. Visiting his father sparked Salva's life mission: building deep-water wells in remote Sudanese villages.

In the novel's final chapter, the two storylines converge. Salva's drilling crew arrives in Nya's village, drilling through hard rock until cool, crystal-clear water gushes into the sunlight. As the villagers celebrate, a new school is built beside the well so that girls like Nya no longer have to spend their childhood hauling water. Stepping forward, Nya extends her hand to the leader of the drilling team: 'Thank you for bringing water.' Smiling, he replies, 'My name is Salva.' A Dinka man had brought life-saving water to a Nuer village, breaking decades of ethnic enmity with unconditional compassion.
